days.label: Tao Te Ching 1
days.key: (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.
days.s: Following the chapter’s opening on the enduring Tao and name, the verse sets out two aspects; Wang Bi, on chapter 1, reads both as the Tao, which begins things while they lack form and name and rears them as their mother once formed and named.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 1, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 2
days.key: All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what ugliness is; they all know the skill of the skilful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what the want of skill is.
days.s: Opening a chapter that sets opposites side by side, the verse gives the first two pairs; Wang Bi, on chapter 2, reads beauty and ugliness as the heart’s delight and loathing, like joy and anger, which share one root, so neither can be singled out.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 2, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 3
days.key: Therefore the sage, in the exercise of his government, empties their minds, fills their bellies, weakens their wills, and strengthens their bones.
days.s: After counsel to keep the people from rivalry and theft, the verse turns to the sage’s rule; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 3, reads it as governing state and self alike, the mind cleared of cravings, the bones firmed by husbanding the vital essence.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 3, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 4
days.key: We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things; we should attemper our brightness, and bring ourselves into agreement with the obscurity of others.
days.s: Between images of the Tao’s emptiness and stillness, the chapter turns to conduct; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 4, takes it as checking the keen pursuit of merit and fame, untying knotted resentment, and sharing the common dust rather than standing apart.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 4, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 5
days.key: Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with.
days.s: The chapter opens here, then says the same of the sages; Wang Bi, on chapter 5, reads it as heaven and earth making nothing and leaving all things to order themselves: earth grows no grass for beasts, yet beasts eat grass.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 5, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 6
days.key: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same; The female mystery thus do we name.
days.s: The chapter opens here, then turns to a gate and root; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 6, reads the valley as nourishing the spirits of the five viscera, and the female mystery as heaven and earth, in a person the nose and mouth.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 6, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 7
days.key: Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place; he treats his person as if it were foreign to him, and yet that person is preserved.
days.s: After heaven and earth, enduring by not living for themselves, the chapter turns to the sage; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 7, reads this as putting others first, taking little for himself and giving much, so the people love him as father and mother.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 7, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 8
days.key: And when (one with the highest excellence) does not wrangle (about his low position), no one finds fault with him.
days.s: The verse closes a chapter that likens the highest excellence to water; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 8, takes the not wrangling as water’s way of going along with people, stopping when dammed and flowing when released, so no one under heaven blames it.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 8, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 9
days.key: When the work is done, and one’s name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.
days.s: After warnings against fullness, sharpness, treasure and arrogance, the chapter ends on success; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 9, reads it as warning that whoever achieves and does not step down meets harm, as the noon sun moves on and the full moon wanes.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 9, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 10
days.key: (The Tao) produces (all things) and nourishes them; it produces them and does not claim them as its own; it does all, and yet does not boast of it; it presides over all, and yet does not control them. This is what is called ‘The mysterious Quality’ (of the Tao).
days.s: Ending a chapter on the souls, the breath and ruling the state, the verse sums up; Wang Bi, on chapter 10, reads producing as not blocking the source of things, nourishing as not restraining their nature, and the mystery as virtue with no master.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 10, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 11
days.key: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends.
days.s: Opening a chapter of three images, with vessel and room to follow, the verse gives the first; Wang Bi, on chapter 11, reads the nave as gathering its spokes through its non-being, which can receive things, and so holding the many together.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 11, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 12
days.key: Therefore the sage seeks to satisfy (the craving of) the belly, and not the (insatiable longing of the) eyes. He puts from him the latter, and prefers to seek the former.
days.s: After the chapter warns how colours, notes, flavours, the hunt and rare objects harm people, the verse draws its lesson; Wang Bi, on chapter 12, reads serving the belly as using things to nourish oneself, and serving the eyes as letting things enslave one.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 12, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 13
days.key: Therefore he who would administer the kingdom, honouring it as he honours his own person, may be employed to govern it, and he who would administer it with the love which he bears to his own person may be entrusted with it.
days.s: Closing a chapter on favour and disgrace, the verse turns to government; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 13, takes the first ruler as prizing himself and scorning others, ruling only briefly, and the second as loving himself for the people’s sake, long without blame.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 13, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 14
days.key: When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, and are able to know it as it was of old in the beginning, this is called (unwinding) the clue of Tao.
days.s: Closing a chapter on the invisible, the verse joins past and present; Wang Bi, on chapter 14, takes that Tao as the formless, nameless ancestor of all things, through which every age achieves order however customs change, so the ancient beginning is knowable now.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 14, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 15
days.key: Shrinking looked they like those who wade through a stream in winter; irresolute like those who are afraid of all around them; grave like a guest (in awe of his host); evanescent like ice that is melting away; unpretentious like wood that has not been fashioned into anything; vacant like a valley, and dull like muddy water.
days.s: Describing the skilful masters of old, the verse strings seven likenesses; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 15, takes the ice as shedding feeling and desire, the wood as spirit kept within without ornament, and the muddy water as merging with the crowd.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 15, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 16
days.key: All things alike go through their processes of activity, and (then) we see them return (to their original state).
days.s: After a call for vacancy and stillness, the chapter turns to things in motion; Wang Bi, on chapter 16, takes the return as seen through emptiness and stillness, to which all things go back at last, since being arises from emptiness and movement from stillness.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 16, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 17
days.key: In the next age they loved them and praised them. In the next they feared them; in the next they despised them.
days.s: Tracing rule from the highest antiquity, the chapter names three later ages; Wang Bi, on chapter 17, takes them as lesser rulers: one who, unable to govern by non-action, bestows favours, one who relies on power, and one who rules by cleverness and is evaded.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 17, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 18
days.key: When the Great Tao (Way or Method) ceased to be observed, benevolence and righteousness came into vogue.
days.s: Opening a chapter where virtues appear as order fails, the verse gives the first; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 18, reads the Great Tao’s age as one of filial sons and good faith, when benevolence and righteousness went unseen until evil and rebellion arose.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 18, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 19
days.key: If we could renounce our sageness and discard our wisdom, it would be better for the people a hundredfold.
days.s: This opens the chapter’s three renunciations, which close on simple views and plain courses; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 19, reads renouncing sageness as giving up the sages’ making to return to the beginning, and discarding wisdom as return to non-action.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 19, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 20
days.key: The multitude of men look satisfied and pleased; as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring. I alone seem listless and still, my desires having as yet given no indication of their presence.
days.s: After renouncing learning, the chapter sets the crowd against its speaker; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 20, reads the crowd’s pleasure as dissolute desire, a hungry man longing for a feast, never satisfied, and the stillness as calm, with no sign of passion yet.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 20, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 21
days.key: How know I that it is so with all the beauties of existing things? By this (nature of the Tao).
days.s: Closing a chapter on the elusive Tao, the text asks and answers; Wang Bi, on chapter 21, reads the question as how all things are known to begin in non-being, and ‘this’ as the account above of the nameless, through which all is completed.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 21, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 22
days.key: The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new.
days.s: Reversals open a chapter on the sage free from self-display; Wang Bi, on chapter 22, reads them as not displaying oneself, not holding oneself right, not boasting and not vaunting oneself, which leave one whole, one’s rightness plain, one’s merit kept and one’s virtue lasting.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 22, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 23
days.key: Abstaining from speech marks him who is obeying the spontaneity of his nature.
days.s: A chapter on passing storms and on following the Tao opens with the verse; Wang Bi, on chapter 23, takes the speech as faint, unheard like the Tao’s flavourless words, and reads it as the utmost speech of what is so of itself.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 23, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 24
days.key: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches his legs does not walk (easily).
days.s: Two images open a chapter on self-display and self-conceit; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 24, takes the first as one greedy for power and fame, who cannot stand long, and the second as striding over others in self-importance till the many block the way.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 24, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 25
days.key: Man takes his law from the Earth; the Earth takes its law from Heaven; Heaven takes its law from the Tao. The law of the Tao is its being what it is.
days.s: Closing a chapter on the formless thing before Heaven and Earth, the verse links four in a chain; Wang Bi, on chapter 25, reads each as not going against the next, and the Tao as going against nothing that is so of itself.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 25, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 26
days.key: Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of movement.
days.s: The chapter opens here, then turns to a prince and his baggage waggons; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 26, reads it for the ruler, not honoured without gravity and losing authority without stillness, and for the self, the spirit lost and the body endangered.
days.src: The Heshang Gong commentary, Laozi Daodejing Heshang Gong zhangju, chapter 26, zh.wikisource (a normalised text), revision 2019760 (2021)

days.label: Tao Te Ching 27
days.key: In the same way the sage is always skilful at saving men, and so he does not cast away any man; he is always skilful at saving things, and so he does not cast away anything.
days.s: After five skilful figures, the chapter turns to the sage; Wang Bi, on chapter 27, reads it as setting no forms and names to check things and no path of advancement to cast off the unworthy, but aiding all things to be so of themselves.
days.src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 27, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)
